articles.title: Samsung Wallet targets U.S. market with rewards card
articles.description: Samsung Electronics is stepping up its push into the U.S. digital payments market with a new credit card offering higher rewards than Apple Card, as the South Korean technology giant seeks to turn users of its smartphones and appliances into financial customers. / Chat GPT Samsung began accepting general applications for its first own-brand credit card, the Samsung Galaxy Card, in the United States on July 22, according to financial and technology industry officials. Consumers can apply online or at Samsung stores across the country. The card is issued by British bank Barclays and runs on Visa’s payment network. It is available as a virtual card in Samsung Wallet and as a black metal physical card. The Galaxy Card offers 5% back on purchases made directly from Samsung and 3% on payments through Samsung Wallet. Subscription services including Netflix, Disney+ and Spotify earn 2%, while all other purchases earn 1%. The card has no annual fee or foreign transaction fees. Its rewards exceed those of Apple Card across key spending categories. Apple Card offers 3% on Apple products, App Store and in-app purchases and transactions with selected merchants. Apple Pay purchases earn 2%, while physical card transactions earn 1%. That puts the Galaxy Card two percentage points ahead on purchases of the company’s own products and one percentage point higher on mobile wallet payments. Samsung is also offering a $200 bonus to customers who spend $2,000 within 90 days of opening an account, equivalent to 10% of the spending requirement. Apple Card does not provide a permanent sign-up bonus. The promotion, combined with the card’s standard rewards, could widen the gap in first-year benefits. Credit card industry officials said products offering unlimited 3% rewards on all mobile wallet transactions without an annual fee were uncommon. While co-branded cards often provide uncapped rewards within a company’s own sales channels, few offer 3% across all merchant categories based solely on the payment method. Samsung’s aggressive incentives come as it seeks to narrow a wide gap with Apple in the U.S. digital wallet market. Samsung Wallet accounts for about 42% of South Korea’s digital wallet market but has a share of roughly 3% in the United States. Apple Pay controls more than half of the U.S. market. Samsung is betting that its broad household presence will support demand for the Galaxy Card. About 70% of U.S. households own at least one Samsung product, while nearly 30% own three or more, according to the company. The strategy is aimed at converting customers gained through smartphones, televisions and home appliances into regular users of Samsung’s financial services. Samsung could eventually expand the Wallet ecosystem by adding digital bank accounts, high-yield savings products and buy-now-pay-later services, industry officials said. jdh@chosunbiz.com

articles.description: Evelyn Hockstein/REUTERS The president of the United States has flooded his Truth Social account with a bizarre AI stream of his digital fever dreams as pressure builds to end his unpopular war in Iran. Donald Trump unleashed a bonkers posting spree Sunday centered around his apparent vision for another term in the White House, firing off 16 consecutive AI-generated or AI-altered images from a reality tailored to his liking. The 80-year-old president began his spree shortly after 11 a.m., when he posted an AI image depicting CNN star Kaitlan Collins as Dylan Mulvaney , a transgender actress despised by MAGA devotees for appearing in Bud Light advertisements. Read more at The Daily Beast.
